# A-440

Elias Vann had been tuning pianos for forty-one years when the high notes began to leave him.

They didn't vanish all at once. First the top octave went soft at the edges, like fruit going over. Then the B above middle C developed a fuzz he couldn't shave off, no matter how carefully he turned the pin. The audiologist used words like *presbycusis* and *noise-induced* and drew a graph that dipped like a bird's wing on the right side. Elias looked at the dip and thought: there goes my living.

He kept working anyway. You'd be surprised, he told people, how much of this job lives in the hands. The keybed carries the vibration up through the wrists. A string pulled true hums differently against the fingertip than one pulled sharp — a kind of brightness, a tautness, like the difference in a handshake between someone glad to see you and someone merely willing. His thumbs had opinions. His teeth, when he pressed the stem of the tuning fork between them, delivered the pitch straight to the bone, past the ruined machinery of his ears entirely.

Still, he grieved. Forty-one years of listening had made him a kind of archivist. He could identify a Steinway from across a room with his eyes shut, could tell a 1910 upright from a 1935 by the particular wear in its tenor register. All of that was closing like a shop. Some nights he lay awake running scales in his head, testing which pitches survived, calling the roll like a teacher checking attendance.

The call came on a Tuesday in October. A woman named Ruth Okafor, out past the county line, wanted the old upright in her parlor tuned before Thanksgiving. Her husband had died in June. He played every evening after dinner, she said, badly, the same twelve songs. She hadn't been able to open the fallboard since.

Elias drove out with his kit in the passenger seat, the mutes and felts and the fork wrapped in flannel like something surgical. The maples along Route 9 were turning; he drove with the windows down out of habit, though the wind had stopped bringing him much news.

The house smelled of dust and lemon polish and, faintly, of cooked onions from years of dinners. The piano stood against the north wall, a Kimball upright from the fifties, walnut veneer gone dull along the edges where sixty years of forearms had leaned. He lifted the fallboard. On the music rack sat sheet music gone soft at the corners: hymns, a few standards, "Danny Boy" annotated in pencil — *slower here*, in a careful hand.

Ruth sat in the kitchen doorway with her coffee while he worked, and talked, the way people do when the silence of a house has grown too large. Harold never met a tempo he respected. Harold's mother made him practice as a boy and he hated it, and then somewhere around retirement the hatred turned into devotion, the way it does. Harold hit middle C so hard the neighbors two houses down learned to set their clocks by it.

Elias nodded along and listened with his whole body. He laid the mutes. He struck the fork and pressed it to the plate and let the hum climb his arm. Note by note he brought the strings into agreement with each other, the intervals settling like furniture into place.

It took him most of the afternoon. When he reached the middle of the keyboard, he stopped.

There was a groove worn into the middle C key — not a scratch, a shallow valley, polished smooth, the lacquer rubbed away in the shape of a thumbprint larger than any single print. Forty years of the same finger landing in the same place, hard, always hard. The hammer felt had compressed beneath it. When he tested the note, it spoke a half-beat faster than its neighbors, bright and insistent, a voice accustomed to being heard.

He could have corrected it. New felt, a lighter touch, even voicing. That was the job. That was what *tuned* meant.

But he sat there a long time with his hand hovering over the key, thinking about what Ruth had said — *the same twelve songs, badly* — and about the pencil note on "Danny Boy," *slower here*, and about how a house learns a sound the way a riverbed learns water, and what it does to a house when the sound stops.

He left the middle C alone. He voiced its neighbors gently around it instead, so that when the chord came, everything would lean toward that one bright note without trying to drown it. Then he closed the lid and packed his tools.

Ruth paid him at the door and asked if it sounded right. He told her the truth, or near enough: that pianos are never finished, only agreed upon. That hers was in agreement now.

She opened the fallboard before he'd reached the car. Through the screen door he heard her play the first bars of "Danny Boy," slower, slower, hunting for the tempo penciled in a dead man's hand. And when she reached the phrase where the melody lands hardest — he knew the phrase; everyone knows the phrase — the middle C rang out ahead of the rest, bright and uncorrected, exactly the way it had rung for forty years, and Ruth laughed once, sharply, the way people laugh when grief turns a corner they weren't watching.

Elias stood in the yard a moment longer than he needed to. The high frequencies were gone from his ears for good, but standing there he heard the note anyway, carried up through the ground, through the air, through whatever part of us listens without ears.

Then he got in the truck and drove home in the long gold light, already forgetting the road, the way you do, when something has gone right.
